title: Nanoscale Mapping of Strain-engineered Excitons in Monolayer WSe$_2$
authors: Anna S. Roche, Nicholas V. Proscia, Paul D. Cunningham, Kathleen M. McCreary, Dante J. O'Hara, Hsun Jen Chuang, Cory Cress, Collin Sanborn, Samuel W. LaGasse, Jose J. Fonseca, Jeremy T. Robinson, Takashi Taniguchi, Kenji Watanabe, John R. Schaibley, Brian J. LeRoy
abstract: Excitons in monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are highly sensitive to external stimuli, allowing control of resonance energies and lifetimes through electric and magnetic fields, heterostructures, moire potentials and mechanical strain. Observations of single-photon emission (SPE) near sample edges, wrinkles, and strained nanobubbles have motivated strain-engineering aimed at realizing localized emitters in 2D materials. The origin of these emitters remains unclear and prior studies have relied on far-field spectroscopy with strain profiles inferred separately through topography, limiting direct correlation between local strain and excitonic response. We directly probe strain-modified excitonic spectra in monolayer WSe$_2$ using cryogenic scattering-type scanning near-field optical microscopy (s-SNOM). We compare two strain-engineering techniques, nano-indentation and patterned substrates, used to produce SPEs. At 9 K, we spatially resolve exciton resonance shifts with sub-diffraction limit resolution, simultaneously measuring near-field optical response and topography. We observe that strain transferred from nano-indentation into a deformable polymer substrate differs from that produced by draping TMDs over patterned dielectric pillars. Adhesion and tearing during plastic deformation drive a compressive exciton blueshift, while draping produces dominant tensile strain. Comparing the strain model results to the experimentally observed energy shifts shows that the nano-indentation strain is over an order of magnitude smaller than previously inferred, due to puncturing of the fragile monolayer, whereas pillar-strained devices remain intact under more modest strain. These differences suggest SPE arises from complex, strain-mediated interactions rather than simple confinement potentials, establishing s-SNOM as a powerful probe of quantum emission in strained 2D materials.
summary: This paper uses advanced near-field microscopy (s-SNOM) to measure how mechanical strain affects excitons in monolayer WSe2. By comparing results from nano-indentation and pillar patterning, the authors demonstrate that prior estimates of strain were overestimated because the material tears before reaching theoretical limits. This establishes s-SNOM as a key tool for understanding strain-mediated quantum emission in 2D materials.
main_problem: The study aims to directly probe and quantify the strain-induced modifications of excitonic spectra in monolayer WSe2, resolving the ambiguity in how localized emitters (SPEs) are formed.
main_result: Direct near-field measurements reveal that the strain experienced by the monolayer is significantly smaller than previously estimated from topography, suggesting that SPEs arise from complex, strain-mediated interactions rather than simple confinement potentials.
method: The researchers employed cryogenic scattering-type scanning near-field optical microscopy (s-SNOM) to simultaneously map near-field optical response and topography while applying controlled mechanical strain via nano-indentation and patterned substrates.
model_or_system: The physical system is monolayer WSe2, a transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD). The analysis involves comparing measured exciton energy shifts against theoretical strain models derived from the substrate deformation (e.g., using force equilibrium equations).
key_observables: Exciton resonance energy shifts ($\Delta E$), near-field amplitude ($s$), phase ($\phi$), and topographical height profiles.
important_parameters: Temperature (9 K), sub-diffraction resolution ($\sim 40$ nm), strain magnitude (comparing observed $\sim 15$ meV shifts vs. predicted $\gg 400$ meV shifts).
main_assumptions: Initial models assumed perfect, continuous strain transfer based on topography, an assumption the paper ultimately refutes by showing material tearing limits the actual strain.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate s-SNOM setups, near-field amplitude/phase maps across indentations, and line scans correlating exciton energy shifts with physical deformation profiles.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the need for direct measurement, details the s-SNOM methodology for comparing two strain techniques (indentation vs. pillar draping), presents the quantitative results showing discrepancies between expected and measured strain, and concludes by refining the understanding of SPE origins.
why_interesting: The work provides a powerful, direct experimental technique (s-SNOM) to map quantum material properties (excitons) under controlled, localized strain, which is crucial for understanding quantum emitters in 2D materials relevant to quantum optics and solid-state quantum information.

A WSe2 is transferred onto a PMMA substrate and an AFM tip creates the indentation, inducing tensile strain and initiating plastic flow of the deformable PMMA (B). The volume conservation during plastic flow creates a rim, which experiences lateral surface displacement causing compression of the adhered WSe2 (C). The resulting strain profile in D is dominated by extreme tensile values, beyond breaking strain, in the crater and compression in the rim.
